headline: All 21 cars tested transmit data to third parties, over half to advertisers
summary: Researchers found every modern vehicle tested sends data to at least one third-party domain, with over half also contacting advertising and analytics firms. This widespread data harvesting highlights a significant lack of owner control.
details: A new study by Northeastern University and Consumer Reports reveals that all 21 modern vehicles tested transmitted data to at least one third-party domain. More than half of these vehicles were found to be sending data to advertising, tracking, or analytics companies.

Modern cars are essentially smartphones on wheels, collecting vast amounts of data on driving habits, location, speed, and more. The legality of this extensive data harvesting is a subject of ongoing debate and regulatory action.

The Federal Trade Commission previously penalized General Motors for illegally collecting and selling location data without consent, while Ford and Honda faced fines for making opt-out processes too difficult. This new research systematically investigates the scale of such practices.

David Choffnes, project lead, stated the goal was to expose the extent of modern vehicle data tracking and the minimal control owners have. He concluded that "there’s a lot to be worried about" regarding automotive data privacy.

To gather data, researchers placed a Raspberry Pi in each car to monitor Wi-Fi traffic, routing it through a mobile hotspot. For cellular traffic, they built a car-sized Faraday tent to force vehicles onto a controlled Wi-Fi connection, avoiding public network interference.

The findings were stark: every single vehicle transmitted data over Wi-Fi to at least one third-party domain. Companies like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude were among those receiving data, which can be used for targeted ads or sold to insurance providers.

Vehicles equipped with advanced infotainment systems, particularly those running Google’s Android Automotive OS, contacted the highest number of third-party domains. This suggests that an automaker's choice of software platform directly influences the volume of data shared with external entities.

The study also highlighted that mobile apps linked to vehicles act as equally insecure vectors for data collection. This trend further solidifies the notion that cars are evolving into sophisticated, global data-harvesting devices, akin to personal smartphones.

headline: AI companies leak data to advertisers
summary: A new report reveals that several AI companies are reportedly sharing user data with advertising partners, raising significant privacy concerns for millions of users.
details: A recent report has uncovered that numerous artificial intelligence companies are reportedly transmitting user data to various advertising entities. This practice raises significant questions regarding user privacy and data protection standards within the AI industry.

The data transfer, detailed in a PDF report, suggests a potential breach of user trust, as personal information could be used for targeted advertising without explicit consent. This could have broad implications for how AI services handle sensitive user information.

Experts are calling for increased scrutiny and regulation of data handling practices by AI firms to ensure user privacy is safeguarded. The findings highlight the ongoing challenge of balancing innovation with robust data security measures.

The report urges users to review the privacy policies of AI services they use and for companies to adopt more transparent data sharing practices. Regulatory bodies may also consider new guidelines to address these emerging privacy concerns.
